# Creating a custom keyboard
Add an extension to your Xcode project to provide systemwide customized text input.

## Overview
A custom keyboard replaces the system keyboard for users who want capabilities such as a novel text input method or the ability to enter text in a language not otherwise supported. Users enable your custom keyboard in Settings, which allows them to access your keyboard systemwide wherever third-party keyboards are supported.
Note
If your keyboard is specific to your app, use a `UIInput View` instead of creating a custom keyboard. Set the `input View` property of text fields or text views to a view that should replace the system keyboard.
Creating a custom keyboard requires several steps. In addition to adding a Custom Keyboard extension target to your project, you have to configure options, implement your custom interface, and decide what text interactions to support. Users expect a variety of common keyboard interactions such as autocorrection, autocapitalization, smart quotes, and more.

...

### Add your custom user interface
When the user activates your keyboard, it replaces the system keyboard. Your custom keyboard extension’s principal class provides the view that’s displayed. By default, Xcode’s custom keyboard template configures a class named `Keyboard View Controller` as the principal class. This controller’s view is where you define your user interface.
Tip
For design guidance, see [Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/components/selection-and-input/onscreen-keyboards) .
When designing your keyboard’s user interface, incorporate a button to switch keyboards. The system keyboard uses a button with a globe icon as shown in the following image.

...

### Handle text interactions
Custom keyboards run in an isolated process that doesn’t have direct access to the text input view. `UIInput View Controller` provides a `text Document Proxy` property allowing your keyboard to access the text input view. You use this proxy to get the selected text, insert or delete text, manipulate the text insertion position, and get surrounding textual context in order to support things like autocorrect or autocomplete.
```
// Insert a string into the text input view. textDocumentProxy.insertText( "Hello world." ) // Get the currently selected text let  selectedText  =  textDocumentProxy.selectedText
```
For more information, see Handling text interactions in custom keyboards .

### Debug your custom keyboard
Debugging a custom keyboard is similar to debugging any app extension. Xcode prompts you to choose a host app to launch, then you begin editing text in that host app in order to invoke your custom keyboard. The host app can be any app available in the run destination, including your app that contains the keyboard extension.
1. Select the build scheme for your keyboard extension target and a run destination (simulator or device).
2. Select Product > Run to begin your debugging session.
3. Xcode prompts you to select a host app. Choose an app that allows text input, like Notes. Xcode builds and installs your app with its keyboard extension, then launches the app you selected.
4. After the host app launches, begin editing a text field. The most recently used keyboard is shown.
5. Touch and hold the globe button to display the list of available keyboards. Choose your app’s keyboard.

# Handling text interactions in custom keyboards
Insert, delete, and manipulate text by using a proxy to a text input view.

## Overview
Custom keyboards execute in a separate process that doesn’t have direct access to the text a user is editing. A proxy object, `UIText Document Proxy` , provides access to the input text view. Through the text document proxy you can insert or delete text, manipulate the insertion point, and access additional textual context around the insertion point.

### Insert and delete text
The text document proxy conforms to the `UIKey Input` protocol, providing methods for inserting and deleting text. To insert a character or string into the current input view:
```
textDocumentProxy.insertText( "Hello world." )
```
To delete the character preceding the current insertion point:
```
textDocumentProxy.deleteBackward()
```
You can determine if the input view has any text at all using the `has Text` property:
```
if  textDocumentProxy.hasText { // Do something with the text }
```

### Adjust the insertion point
To move the insertion point in the text input view, use the `adjust Text Position(by Character Offset:)` method. For example, if you want to implement a forward delete action, move the insertion position forward by one character then delete backwards:
```
// Move the text insertion position forward 1 character textDocumentProxy.adjustTextPosition(byCharacterOffset:  1 ) // Delete the previous character textDocumentProxy.deleteBackward()
```
You might choose to enable this capability only when the insertion point isn’t at the end of the text being input by checking the context after the insertion point. See Get context around the insertion point for more details.

...

### Get context around the insertion point
To perform certain operations like autocomplete or autocapitalization, you may need additional context of the text surrounding what the user is typing. You can access the context before and after the insertion point as follows:
```
let  precedingText  =  textDocumentProxy.documentContextBeforeInput  ?? "" let  followingText  =  textDocumentProxy.documentContextAfterInput  ?? "" let  selectedText  =  textDocumentProxy.selectedText  ?? "" let  fullText  = " \(precedingText) \(selectedText) \(followingText) "
```
Use `CFString Tokenizer` to better understand the context by breaking the surrounding text (or combined text) into words, paragraphs, or sentences. This information enables you to implement autocapitalization.

...

### Mark text while the user is editing
Some text input operations require multiple actions in order to complete a single character or word. For example, your keyboard might support a language that requires multiple keystrokes to compose a single character. `UIText Document Proxy` allows you to insert text and mark some or all of it for subsequent editing operations. The following code shows how you could insert a combining accent character as marked text using `set Marked Text(_: selected Range:)` :
```
let  accentCharacter  = "  \u{0301} " let  range  = NSRange (location:  0 , length: accentCharacter.count) textDocumentProxy.setMarkedText(accentCharacter, selectedRange: range)
```
Calling `set Marked Text` selects the text specified by `range` . Subsequent insertions replace the characters selected in the range. In the example above, a space with a combining acute accent is shown. If the next character input by the user is an `a` , you could then insert a combined `á` .
```
textDocumentProxy.insertText( "a \u{0301} " )
```
If the range passed to `set Marked Text(_: selected Range:)` only covers a portion of the string passed in, the nonselected portion is marked with a background color. You could use this to display autocompleted content. For example, if you supported autocompletion of names and the user had typed “Anth”, you might display “Anthony” as the autocompletion:
```
let  text  = "Anthony" let  range  = NSRange (location:  4 , length:  3 ) textDocumentProxy.setMarkedText(text, selectedRange: range)
```
The above would display the text as:
As the user continues to type, you can update the marked text with subsequent calls to `set Marked Text(_: selected Range:)` .
Call `unmark Text()` to clear the marked text indication, leaving the text in the input view.

3: // Lex iOS keyboard extension.
4: //
5: // Adapts the macOS app's idea (engine-driven synthetic-backspace + replacement
6: // reconciliation, with liblex as the single source of truth) to a custom
7: // keyboard. There is no CGEventTap here: the extension *is* the keyboard, so it
8: // reconciles against the host text field through UITextDocumentProxy
9: // (insertText / deleteBackward) instead of synthesising key events.
10: //
11: // File layout:
12: //   - LexEngine            : thin Swift wrapper over the liblex C ABI.
13: //   - KeyboardViewController: UIInputViewController principal class; owns the
14: //                             engine and the tap-to-text reconciliation logic.
15: //   - KeyboardView          : from-scratch UIKit US-QWERTY UI (3 planes).
16: 
17: // MARK: - Engine wrapper
18: 
19: // Thin wrapper over the liblex C ABI. Pure C interop, no UIKit; mirrors the
20: // macOS app's LexEngine so the proven behaviour carries over verbatim.
21: private final class LexEngine {
22:     // The internal state of the engine. DO NOT READ.
23:     private let state: UnsafeMutableRawPointer
24:     // The memory to receive the replacement characters from engine.
25:     private var replacement_buffer: [UInt16] = [UInt16](
26:         repeating: 0,
27:         count: Int(lex_replacement_buffer_length)
28:     )
29:     // The memory to receive the number of replacement characters from engine.
30:     private var replacement_count: UInt8 = 0
31: 
32:     init() {
33:         let byte_count = Int(lex_state_size)
34:         let alignment = Int(lex_state_alignment)
35:         let state = UnsafeMutableRawPointer.allocate(
36:             byteCount: byte_count,
37:             alignment: alignment
38:         )
39:         lex_init(state)
40:         self.state = state
41:     }
42: 
43:     deinit {
44:         self.state.deallocate()
45:     }
46: 
47:     func reset() {
48:         lex_init(self.state)
49:     }
50: 
51:     func add(_ unicode_scalar: Unicode.Scalar) {
52:         guard unicode_scalar.isASCII else {
53:             return
54:         }
55:         lex_add(self.state, UInt8(unicode_scalar.value))
56:     }
57: 
58:     func backspace() {
59:         if !self.buffer_empty() {
60:             lex_backspace(self.state)
61:         }
62:     }
63: 
64:     func buffer_full() -> Bool {

66:     }

70:     }

81:     // the engine produced at least one character.
82:     func compose_replacement(_ body: (UnsafeBufferPointer<UInt16>) -> Void) {
83:         self.replacement_count = 0
84:         lex_compose_utf16_string_replacement(
85:             self.state,
86:             &self.replacement_buffer,

533:     // MARK: Layout

535:     override func layoutSubviews() {
536:         super.layoutSubviews()
537: 
538:         let edge: CGFloat = 6.5
539:         let gap: CGFloat = 6
540:         let top_inset: CGFloat = 8
541:         let bottom_inset = max(self.safeAreaInsets.bottom, 4)
542:         let row_gap: CGFloat = 11
543:         let width = self.bounds.width
544: 
545:         guard width > 0, self.rows.count == 4 else {
546:             return
547:         }
548: 
549:         let available_height = self.bounds.height - top_inset - bottom_inset
550:         let row_height = (available_height - row_gap * 3) / 4
551:         // Key unit derived from the 10-key top row so every letter key matches
552:         // the system keyboard's width and narrower rows centre naturally.
553:         let key_unit = (width - 2 * edge - 9 * gap) / 10
554: 
555:         for (index, row) in self.rows.enumerated() {
556:             let y = top_inset + CGFloat(index) * (row_height + row_gap)
557:             self.layout_row(
558:                 row,
559:                 y: y,
560:                 row_height: row_height,
561:                 key_unit: key_unit,
562:                 gap: gap,
563:                 edge: edge,
564:                 total_width: width
565:             )
566:         }
567: 
568:         self.layout_hit_frames()

571:     private func resolved_width(_ width: KeyWidth, key_unit: CGFloat) -> CGFloat? {
572:         switch width {
573:         case .unit:
574:             return key_unit
575:         case .ratio(let ratio):
576:             return key_unit * ratio
577:         case .fill:
578:             return nil
579:         }
580:     }

582:     private func layout_row(
583:         _ row: [KeyButton],
584:         y: CGFloat,
585:         row_height: CGFloat,
586:         key_unit: CGFloat,
587:         gap: CGFloat,
588:         edge: CGFloat,
589:         total_width: CGFloat
590:     ) {
591:         var fixed_sum: CGFloat = 0
592:         var fill_count = 0
593:         for button in row {
594:             if let resolved = self.resolved_width(button.cap.width, key_unit: key_unit) {
595:                 fixed_sum += resolved
596:             } else {
597:                 fill_count += 1
598:             }
599:         }
600: 
601:         let total_gap = gap * CGFloat(max(row.count - 1, 0))
602:         let row_available = total_width - 2 * edge
603: 
604:         var fill_width: CGFloat = 0
605:         if fill_count > 0 {
606:             fill_width = max((row_available - fixed_sum - total_gap) / CGFloat(fill_count), key_unit)
607:         }
608: 
609:         // Rows with a fill key start at the edge and span the width; rows
610:         // without (the letter rows) are centred so row 2 indents like iOS.
611:         var x: CGFloat = (fill_count > 0) ? edge : (total_width - (fixed_sum + total_gap)) / 2
612: 
613:         for button in row {
614:             let button_width = self.resolved_width(button.cap.width, key_unit: key_unit) ?? fill_width
615:             button.frame = CGRect(x: x, y: y, width: button_width, height: row_height)
616:             x += button_width + gap
617:         }
618:     }

620:     private func layout_hit_frames() {
621:         for (row_index, row) in self.rows.enumerated() {
622:             guard !row.isEmpty else {
623:                 continue
624:             }
625: 
626:             let row_top: CGFloat
627:             if row_index == 0 {
628:                 row_top = self.bounds.minY
629:             } else {
630:                 let previous_row = self.rows[row_index - 1]
631:                 row_top = (previous_row[0].frame.maxY + row[0].frame.minY) / 2
632:             }
633: 
634:             let row_bottom: CGFloat
635:             if row_index == self.rows.count - 1 {
636:                 row_bottom = self.bounds.maxY
637:             } else {
638:                 let next_row = self.rows[row_index + 1]
639:                 row_bottom = (row[0].frame.maxY + next_row[0].frame.minY) / 2
640:             }
641: 
642:             for (button_index, button) in row.enumerated() {
643:                 let hit_left: CGFloat
644:                 if button_index == 0 {
645:                     hit_left = self.bounds.minX
646:                 } else {
647:                     let previous_button = row[button_index - 1]
648:                     hit_left = (previous_button.frame.maxX + button.frame.minX) / 2
649:                 }
650: 
651:                 let hit_right: CGFloat
652:                 if button_index == row.count - 1 {
653:                     hit_right = self.bounds.maxX
654:                 } else {
655:                     let next_button = row[button_index + 1]
656:                     hit_right = (button.frame.maxX + next_button.frame.minX) / 2
657:                 }
658: 
659:                 button.hit_frame = CGRect(
660:                     x: hit_left,
661:                     y: row_top,
662:                     width: hit_right - hit_left,
663:                     height: row_bottom - row_top
664:                 )
665:             }
666:         }
667:     }

671:     override func touchesBegan(_ touches: Set<UITouch>, with event: UIEvent?) {
672:         for touch in touches {
673:             let point = touch.location(in: self)
674:             guard let button = self.key_button(at: point) else {
675:                 continue
676:             }
677: 
678:             let touch_id = ObjectIdentifier(touch)
679:             self.active_touches[touch_id] = ActiveTouch(button: button, inside: true)
680:             button.isHighlighted = true
681:             self.key_touch_down(button, touch_id: touch_id)
682:         }
683:     }

685:     override func touchesMoved(_ touches: Set<UITouch>, with event: UIEvent?) {
686:         for touch in touches {
687:             let touch_id = ObjectIdentifier(touch)
688:             guard var active_touch = self.active_touches[touch_id] else {
689:                 continue
690:             }
691: 
692:             let point = touch.location(in: self)
693:             let inside = self.point(point, inside: active_touch.button)
694:             if inside != active_touch.inside {
695:                 active_touch.inside = inside
696:                 active_touch.button.isHighlighted = inside
697:                 self.active_touches[touch_id] = active_touch
698: 
699:                 if !inside, case .backspace = active_touch.button.cap.action {
700:                     active_touch.cancelled = true
701:                     self.active_touches[touch_id] = active_touch
702:                     self.stop_backspace_repeat(touch_id: touch_id)
703:                 }
704:             }
705:         }
706:     }

708:     override func touchesEnded(_ touches: Set<UITouch>, with event: UIEvent?) {
709:         for touch in touches {
710:             let touch_id = ObjectIdentifier(touch)
711:             guard let active_touch = self.active_touches.removeValue(forKey: touch_id) else {
712:                 continue
713:             }
714: 
715:             active_touch.button.isHighlighted = false
716: 
717:             if case .backspace = active_touch.button.cap.action {
718:                 self.stop_backspace_repeat(touch_id: touch_id)
719:             } else if !active_touch.cancelled {
720:                 self.key_tapped(active_touch.button)
721:             }
722:         }
723: 
724:         self.flush_pending_reload_if_idle()
725:     }
726: 
727:     override func touchesCancelled(_ touches: Set<UITouch>, with event: UIEvent?) {
728:         for touch in touches {
729:             let touch_id = ObjectIdentifier(touch)
730:             guard let active_touch = self.active_touches.removeValue(forKey: touch_id) else {
731:                 continue
732:             }
733: 
734:             active_touch.button.isHighlighted = false
735:             if case .backspace = active_touch.button.cap.action {
736:                 self.stop_backspace_repeat(touch_id: touch_id)
737:             }
738:         }
739: 
740:         self.flush_pending_reload_if_idle()
741:     }

743:     private func key_button(at point: CGPoint) -> KeyButton? {
744:         for row in self.rows {
745:             for button in row {
746:                 if self.point(point, inside: button) {
747:                     return button
748:                 }
749:             }
750:         }
751: 
752:         var best_button: KeyButton?
753:         var best_distance = CGFloat.greatestFiniteMagnitude
754:         for row in self.rows {
755:             for button in row {
756:                 let frame = button.hit_frame ?? button.frame
757:                 guard !frame.isEmpty else {
758:                     continue
759:                 }
760: 
761:                 let dx = max(max(frame.minX - point.x, 0), point.x - frame.maxX)
762:                 let dy = max(max(frame.minY - point.y, 0), point.y - frame.maxY)
763:                 let distance = dx * dx + dy * dy
764:                 if distance < best_distance {
765:                     best_distance = distance
766:                     best_button = button
767:                 }
768:             }
769:         }
770: 
771:         return best_button
772:     }

775:         let frame = button.hit_frame ?? button.frame
776:         return frame.contains(point)

The following issues, constraints, and findings were discussed in the thread regarding `Keyboard.swift` fast typing/lost keys and keyboard height/lifecycle problems:

### 1. Fast Typing / Lost Keys (Shift and Space)
* **Context & Suspected Issues:** Fast/overlapping typing often lands a second touch (like a letter) before the first touch (like Space or Shift) is fully released. Because `KeyboardView` was routing touches manually and emitting character actions only on `touchesEnded`, fast-typing sequences could easily be dropped, reordered, or misaligned (e.g., a one-shot Shift reverting at the wrong moment).
* **Proposed Findings/Solutions:** Move character tap detection and dispatch to **`touchesBegan`** (the moment the finger lands) instead of waiting for `touchesEnded`, matching native keyboard touch-down dispatching behavior and ensuring characters are processed immediately in chronological order.

### 2. Custom Keyboard Height / Lifecycle Problems (Whole Screen / Blank Space)
* **Context & Constraints:** Upon hiding and reopening the app, the custom keyboard extension would occasionally take up the whole screen or leave a massive blank area.
* **Proposed Findings/Solutions:** The self-sizing implementation in `loadView` using a `UIInputView` with `allowsSelfSizing = true` and a height constraint of priority `999` was fighting UIKit's internal layout lifecycle. A more robust approach is to let `UIInputViewController` handle its own root view and explicitly define and update the height constraint on the primary view during layout lifecycle steps (such as `viewDidLayoutSubviews` or `updateViewConstraints`) so that the host app correctly respects the height bounds across suspend/resume states.

By default, iOS sizes custom keyboards to match the system keyboard according to screen size and device orientation. # ios-app — Lex iOS keyboard extension

An iOS custom keyboard for the Lex Telex Vietnamese input engine. It adapts the
macOS app's idea — engine-driven synthetic-backspace + replacement
reconciliation with `liblex` as the single source of truth — to a custom
keyboard extension. There is no `CGEventTap`: the extension *is* the keyboard,
so it reconciles against the host text field through `UITextDocumentProxy`
(`insertText` / `deleteBackward`) instead of synthesising key events.

## Architecture

```
╭──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ KeyboardView (UIKit)  — from-scratch US-QWERTY, 3 planes  │
╰───────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────╯
                │ KeyAction (tap events)
╭───────────────▼──────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ KeyboardViewController (UIInputViewController)             │
│  reconciliation: delete N + insert composed replacement   │
╰───────────────┬───────────────────────┬──────────────────╯
        C ABI   │                        │ textDocumentProxy
╭───────────────▼─────────╮   ╭──────────▼──────────────────╮
│ LexEngine (Swift wrap)  │   │ host app text field          │
│ over liblex C ABI       │   ╰──────────────────────────────╯
╰─────────────────────────╯
```

- The engine knows nothing about iOS; the UI knows nothing about Telex; the
  view controller is the only place that reconciles engine state with text
  proxy operations.
- Per letter tap (ASCII a–z/A–Z): feed the engine, `deleteBackward` the
  engine-reported synthetic-backspace count, then insert the composed
  replacement. Digits/symbols/space/return reset the composition and insert
  literally. Lex is always Telex; to type plain Latin or another language the
  user switches keyboards with the globe key.
- An external-change guard (compare `documentContextBeforeInput` against the
  suffix we believe we own) resets the engine when the cursor or text moves
  under us. The keyboard is **not** reset on every `textDidChange`, which would
  break multi-key composition.

## Project layout

```
playground/ios-app/
├── src/                  # liblex snapshot (lex.zig + lex.h), self-contained
├── ios/
│   ├── Lex.swift         # container app (enable-instructions only)
│   ├── Keyboard.swift    # extension: UIInputViewController + UI + engine wrap
│   ├── project.yaml      # xcodegen spec (app + app-extension)
│   ├── Generated/        # xcodegen-injected Info.plists (generated)
│   └── Lex.xcodeproj/    # xcodegen output (generated)
├── build.zig / build.zig.zon
└── README.md
```

`liblex` is immutable upstream (`../../src`). `src/` here is a self-contained
snapshot of that engine; do not edit it.

## Prerequisites

- **Zig 0.15.2** (`.tool-versions`). Builds the `liblex` iOS slices; works on
  Linux and macOS.
- **macOS + Xcode 26** (iOS 26 SDK) for the app/extension build and the
  XCFramework.
- **XcodeGen** (`brew install xcodegen`) — generates the `.xcodeproj` so Xcode
  the IDE is never required.
- Target: **iPhone 11 Pro, iOS 26** (simulator and device). Dev machine for the
  Apple steps is assumed to be Apple Silicon (M1 Pro).

## Build

### On Linux (engine only)

```sh
zig build          # cross-compiles liblex device + simulator slices
zig build test     # runs the liblex unit tests on the host
```

This produces, under `zig-out/`:
`lib/ios-device/liblex.a`, `lib/ios-sim/liblex.a`, `include/lex.h`.
The Xcode-dependent steps print a notice and do nothing on Linux.

### On macOS (full app)

One command does slices → XCFramework → project generation → simulator build:

```sh
zig build app
```

Equivalent explicit steps:

```sh
# 1. Build the liblex iOS slices (device + simulator).
zig build

# 2. Assemble liblex.xcframework (repacks archives with Apple's ar, then
#    xcodebuild -create-xcframework). Output: zig-out/liblex.xcframework
zig build xcframework

# 3. Generate the Xcode project from the spec.
cd ios && xcodegen generate --spec project.yaml && cd ..

# 4. Build the app + keyboard extension for the iPhone 11 Pro simulator.
xcodebuild \
  -project ios/Lex.xcodeproj \
  -scheme Lex \
  -configuration Debug \
  -sdk iphonesimulator \
  -destination 'platform=iOS Simulator,name=iPhone 11 Pro' \
  -derivedDataPath ios/build \
  CODE_SIGNING_ALLOWED=NO \
  build
```

### Run in the simulator

```sh
xcrun simctl boot "iPhone 11 Pro"
open -a Simulator
xcrun simctl install booted \
  ios/build/Build/Products/Debug-iphonesimulator/Lex.app
xcrun simctl launch booted <redacted:bundle-id>
```

Enable the keyboard inside the simulator: **Settings → General → Keyboard →
Keyboards → Add New Keyboard… → Lex**. Then in any text field long-press the
globe key and pick Lex. Lex always types Vietnamese (Telex); switch keyboards
with the globe key to type anything else.

### Build for a device (iPhone 11 Pro)

Device builds require code signing. Provide your Apple development team's
certificate subject `OU` as `DEVELOPMENT_TEAM` and let Xcode manage signing
automatically:

```sh
zig build xcframework
cd ios && xcodegen generate --spec project.yaml && cd ..
xcodebuild \
  -project ios/Lex.xcodeproj \
  -scheme Lex \
  -configuration Release \
  -sdk iphoneos \
  -destination 'generic/platform=iOS' \
  -derivedDataPath ios/build \
  -allowProvisioningUpdates \
  -allowProvisioningDeviceRegistration \
  DEVELOPMENT_TEAM=YOUR_TEAM_ID \
  build
```

Use the `OU` field from the Apple Development certificate subject as the Team ID
for `DEVELOPMENT_TEAM`. Do not copy the id shown in the `security find-identity`
display name; that value can differ from the certificate subject `OU` that
Xcode expects for automatic provisioning.

One way to inspect the certificate subject is:

```sh
security find-certificate \
  -c "<redacted:apple-signing>" \
  -p \
  <redacted:path> |
openssl x509 -noout -subject -nameopt sep_multiline
```

Use the printed `OU = ...` value as `YOUR_TEAM_ID`. The device must be
registered with that team; a free personal team works for local installs. For a
new device, build once with a concrete device destination, for example
`-destination 'platform=iOS,id=DEVICE_UDID'`, so
`-allowProvisioningDeviceRegistration` can register it.

### Install on a device

After a successful device build, install the built app with `devicectl`:

```sh
xcrun devicectl device install app \
  --device DEVICE_UDID \
  ios/build/Build/Products/Release-iphoneos/Lex.app
```

If the app path differs, find it with:

```sh
find ios/build -name Lex.app -type d
```

Launch the container app with the bundle id from `project.yaml`:

```sh
xcrun devicectl device process launch \
  --device DEVICE_UDID \
  <redacted:bundle-id>
```

If you changed `PRODUCT_BUNDLE_IDENTIFIER` in `project.yaml`, use that app
bundle id instead of `<redacted:bundle-id>`. Then enable the keyboard on the
iPhone in **Settings → General → Keyboard → Keyboards → Add New Keyboard… →
Lex**.

## Notes

- **No "Allow Full Access".** `RequestsOpenAccess` is `false`. Basic
  insert/delete needs no special access, so no App Group is used.
- **`liblex` cross-compiles on Linux.** It is pure Zig with a C ABI and no libc
  or Apple-SDK dependency. The slices are tagged `PLATFORM_IOS` (device) and
  `PLATFORM_IOSSIMULATOR` (simulator), both `minos` iOS 26.0.
- **Archive repacking.** Apple's linker rejects non-8-byte-aligned archive
  members produced by Zig, so each slice is repacked with the system `ar` during
  the `xcframework` step (on macOS, to use Apple's `ar`).
- **Stripped slices.** The iOS slices are built `ReleaseSafe` but with
  `strip = true`. This keeps the runtime safety checks while dead-code-removing
  Zig's panic stack-trace symbolizer, which references the dyld SPI
  `_dyld_get_image_header_containing_address` that the iOS SDK refuses to link
  against (an unstripped slice fails to link into the extension). On a panic the
  engine still aborts; it just cannot print a symbolicated trace.
- **Scope (v1).** Portrait only; no predictive bar, long-press alternates, swipe
  typing, or autocorrect. US-QWERTY layout with `123`/`#+=` planes, shift /
  caps-lock, backspace auto-repeat, and globe (next keyboard). Always Telex.
```

## TL;DR

Static review of `Keyboard.swift` looks mostly correct; no obvious Swift syntax or UIKit API compile blockers stood out. Before finalizing, I would make two small lifecycle/UIKit cleanups: move `super.updateViewConstraints()` to the end of the override, and add a `deinit` timer invalidation in `KeyboardView`.

## Recommended approach

Effort: **S, <1h**

1. **Keep the current touch-down emission model.**  
   The `touchesBegan` timestamp sorting, immediate key emission, current `shift_state` character calculation, and `touch_id`-guarded backspace repeat logic are directionally correct for the fast-typing/drop issue.

2. **Move `super.updateViewConstraints()` to the end.**  
   UIKit’s normal Auto Layout override pattern is to update constraints first, then call `super`.

   ```swift
   override func updateViewConstraints() {
       if self.keyboard_height_constraint == nil {
           let height_constraint = self.view.heightAnchor.constraint(
               equalToConstant: Self.keyboard_height
           )
           height_constraint.priority = UILayoutPriority(999)
           height_constraint.isActive = true
           self.keyboard_height_constraint = height_constraint
       }

       self.keyboard_height_constraint?.constant = Self.keyboard_height

       super.updateViewConstraints()
   }
   ```

3. **Add a defensive timer cleanup.**

   ```swift
   deinit {
       self.backspace_timer?.invalidate()
   }
   ```

   `viewWillDisappear`/`cancel_tracking()` should cover normal lifecycle, but a `Timer` scheduled on the run loop can otherwise outlive the view if deallocation happens through an unusual path.

4. **Manual-test these cases on Xcode/device before finalizing:**

   - hide app / reopen keyboard: no full-screen blank keyboard geometry
   - fast overlapping taps: `a s d`, Shift + letter, Shift then two fast letters
   - one-shot Shift reverts correctly while UI reload is delayed
   - caps lock double-tap still works
   - backspace tap, hold-repeat, move finger outside, lift
   - globe / next keyboard key
   - plane switching `123` / `ABC` while another touch is still down

## Rationale and trade-offs

The applied changes are internally consistent:

- `cancel_tracking()` on appear/disappear correctly clears stale active touches and invalidates repeat state.
- Emitting on `touchesBegan` avoids the common software-keyboard race where fast overlapping touches end out of order or get cancelled before `touchesEnded`.
- Computing character text from `self.shift_state` avoids stale `KeyCap` casing while `reload()` is deferred by active touches.
- Guarding backspace timers by `touch_id` prevents an old timer from continuing after its touch ended or was cancelled.

The main trade-off is intentional: keys are now **non-cancelable after touch-down**. If a touch begins on the wrong key and moves away or gets cancelled, the character/action has already been emitted. That is acceptable if dropped fast keys are the higher-priority problem.

## Risks and guardrails

- **UIKit constraint lifecycle:** current `super.updateViewConstraints()` order is not ideal. It likely works, but move it to the end to match UIKit expectations.
- **Timer lifecycle:** normal paths invalidate the backspace timer, but `deinit` cleanup is cheap and safer.
- **Same-key multi-touch highlight:** if two touches are active on the same button, one touch ending will clear the button highlight even if the other remains. This is a minor visual edge, not an input correctness blocker.
- **Multi-finger backspace:** only one `repeating_backspace_touch` is tracked. A second backspace finger can take over repeat ownership; if it lifts while the first remains down, repeat stops. Probably acceptable for a keyboard v1.
- **Plane changes while touches are active:** `reload()` is deferred, so the visible keyboard can temporarily disagree with `self.plane`. Shift letters are handled, but plane-chord behavior is not robust. This is acceptable unless users are expected to tap `123` and immediately type on the new plane before lifting.

## When to consider the advanced path

Only revisit the input model if testing shows real issues with touch-down semantics, such as frequent accidental characters from touches that move outside keys, or users relying on slide-to-cancel behavior.

An advanced path would split behavior by key type:

- emit normal character keys on touch-down,
- emit destructive/navigation keys only after confirming the touch remains inside,
- maintain per-button active-touch counts for highlight correctness,
- model pending plane changes separately from the currently rendered plane.

That is unnecessary unless manual device testing exposes those specific problems.

## TL;DR

Static review of `Keyboard.swift` looks mostly correct; no obvious Swift syntax or UIKit API compile blockers stood out. Before finalizing, I would make two small lifecycle/UIKit cleanups: move `super.updateViewConstraints()` to the end of the override, and add a `deinit` timer invalidation in `KeyboardView`.

## Recommended approach

Effort: **S, <1h**

1. **Keep the current touch-down emission model.**  
   The `touchesBegan` timestamp sorting, immediate key emission, current `shift_state` character calculation, and `touch_id`-guarded backspace repeat logic are directionally correct for the fast-typing/drop issue.

2. **Move `super.updateViewConstraints()` to the end.**  
   UIKit’s normal Auto Layout override pattern is to update constraints first, then call `super`.

   ```swift
   override func updateViewConstraints() {
       if self.keyboard_height_constraint == nil {
           let height_constraint = self.view.heightAnchor.constraint(
               equalToConstant: Self.keyboard_height
           )
           height_constraint.priority = UILayoutPriority(999)
           height_constraint.isActive = true
           self.keyboard_height_constraint = height_constraint
       }

       self.keyboard_height_constraint?.constant = Self.keyboard_height

       super.updateViewConstraints()
   }
   ```

3. **Add a defensive timer cleanup.**

   ```swift
   deinit {
       self.backspace_timer?.invalidate()
   }
   ```

   `viewWillDisappear`/`cancel_tracking()` should cover normal lifecycle, but a `Timer` scheduled on the run loop can otherwise outlive the view if deallocation happens through an unusual path.

4. **Manual-test these cases on Xcode/device before finalizing:**

   - hide app / reopen keyboard: no full-screen blank keyboard geometry
   - fast overlapping taps: `a s d`, Shift + letter, Shift then two fast letters
   - one-shot Shift reverts correctly while UI reload is delayed
   - caps lock double-tap still works
   - backspace tap, hold-repeat, move finger outside, lift
   - globe / next keyboard key
   - plane switching `123` / `ABC` while another touch is still down

## Rationale and trade-offs

The applied changes are internally consistent:

- `cancel_tracking()` on appear/disappear correctly clears stale active touches and invalidates repeat state.
- Emitting on `touchesBegan` avoids the common software-keyboard race where fast overlapping touches end out of order or get cancelled before `touchesEnded`.
- Computing character text from `self.shift_state` avoids stale `KeyCap` casing while `reload()` is deferred by active touches.
- Guarding backspace timers by `touch_id` prevents an old timer from continuing after its touch ended or was cancelled.

The main trade-off is intentional: keys are now **non-cancelable after touch-down**. If a touch begins on the wrong key and moves away or gets cancelled, the character/action has already been emitted. That is acceptable if dropped fast keys are the higher-priority problem.

## Risks and guardrails

- **UIKit constraint lifecycle:** current `super.updateViewConstraints()` order is not ideal. It likely works, but move it to the end to match UIKit expectations.
- **Timer lifecycle:** normal paths invalidate the backspace timer, but `deinit` cleanup is cheap and safer.
- **Same-key multi-touch highlight:** if two touches are active on the same button, one touch ending will clear the button highlight even if the other remains. This is a minor visual edge, not an input correctness blocker.
- **Multi-finger backspace:** only one `repeating_backspace_touch` is tracked. A second backspace finger can take over repeat ownership; if it lifts while the first remains down, repeat stops. Probably acceptable for a keyboard v1.
- **Plane changes while touches are active:** `reload()` is deferred, so the visible keyboard can temporarily disagree with `self.plane`. Shift letters are handled, but plane-chord behavior is not robust. This is acceptable unless users are expected to tap `123` and immediately type on the new plane before lifting.

## When to consider the advanced path

Only revisit the input model if testing shows real issues with touch-down semantics, such as frequent accidental characters from touches that move outside keys, or users relying on slide-to-cancel behavior.

An advanced path would split behavior by key type:

- emit normal character keys on touch-down,
- emit destructive/navigation keys only after confirming the touch remains inside,
- maintain per-button active-touch counts for highlight correctness,
- model pending plane changes separately from the currently rendered plane.

That is unnecessary unless manual device testing exposes those specific problems.
